article_title: Anthony Vaccarello's decade at Saint Laurent: A retrospective
sub_title: As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 1...
article_content: Automated translation As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 10-year career with the Kering group as artistic director for the house of Saint Laurent. It was a high-risk succession. Slimane had been untouchable since the Dior Hommes miracle. He transformed Saint Laurent by removing the first name Yves, giving the brand his own rock aesthetic and crowning his approach with economic success. Turnover almost tripled under the Slimane era, rising from 353.7 million euros in 2011, the year before his arrival, to 974 million euros in 2015, according to the annual reports of PPR/Kering. At the time, Vaccarello was 34 years old and closed his own house to devote himself to Saint Laurent. His time at Versus Versace was his most visible experience at a major house. His first spring/summer 2017 show was therefore highly anticipated and scrutinised by a fashion world always eager for commentary. He followed in the footsteps of his predecessor – with black, leather and transparency – and those of the original couturier, Yves Saint Laurent – the tuxedo, 80s shoulders, leopard print, gold lamé and the YSL/Cassandre monogram. For the spring/summer 2018 collection show, Anthony Vaccarello set up at the Trocadéro, with the illuminated Eiffel Tower as a backdrop. This first visual signature orchestrated the brand's international influence: Saint Laurent is Paris, Paris is Saint Laurent. It was not until the young artistic director met Yves Saint Laurent's muse and best friend, Betty Catroux, that the artistic spark was truly ignited. Anthony Vaccarello met her at the inauguration of the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Marrakech. “She is Saint Laurent as she breathes. Her allure, her mystery, her scandalous side, an elusive and desirable danger, all contribute to the aura of this house. You understand the scale of it when you meet Betty,” explained Vaccarello in the context of an exhibition dedicated to this muse in 2020, at the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Paris. Just as the Saint Laurent/Bergé duo embodied the Parisian Rive Gauche, Vaccarello has made the Rive Droite his own. At the end of his career, Yves Saint Laurent said: “I am just a name. A perfume, a lipstick, a pair of tights”. At the beginning of his, Vaccarello expanded the Saint Laurent universe to include lifestyle and developed a brand image that includes art, photography, music, design and various collaborations. Like a conductor, he put his name to the architectural design of Saint Laurent Rive Droite. On the eve of the Covid-19 crisis, Vaccarello presented a show dominated by red, a premonitory colour that would be found in social news. For autumn/winter 2020/2021, the red is as ardent as the bourgeois woman who cheats the monotony of her days with torrid nights. Vaccarello presents this stage as “a defining moment in the definition of his Saint Laurent woman” (W Magazine, 2025). Classic jackets, pussy-bow blouses, lace, vinyl, latex: Vaccarello explores the inherent sensuality of the Saint Laurent woman. Between glamour and provocation, this power of seduction was then imposed in all his campaigns. From spring/summer 2023, the artistic director evolved the Saint Laurent man. To design his wardrobe, he once again drew on the heritage of Betty Catroux and her masculine-feminine style. Pussy-bow blouses, jackets worn next to the skin, leopard prints, soft fabrics, drapes, asymmetries, transparent shirts and fluid trousers are all distinctive signs of a deconstructed man. Six years after Anthony Vaccarello's arrival as artistic director, Saint Laurent crossed the three billion euro turnover threshold for the first time. Sales reached 3.3 billion euros in 2022, compared to 1.22 billion in 2016. At the same time, recurring operating income exceeded one billion euros, for a margin of 30.9 percent. Source: Kering annual results. The first couture house to venture into film financing, Saint Laurent under the Vaccarello era began with a first short film, “Strange Way of Life”, by Madrid-based director Pedro Almodóvar. The masterstroke came at the 2023 Cannes Film Festival, with three films in competition, including “Emilia Pérez” by Jacques Audiard, which won numerous awards, including the Jury Prize and the collective Best Actress award at Cannes. Some say that the branded costumes (the famous Rive Gauche T-shirt worn by Selena Gomez in Emilia Pérez) and the polished aesthetic blur the line between the director's artistic choices and the brand's expression. The tone has been set: Vaccarello has invented a way of investing in cinema other than product placement. Vaccarello celebrates 10 years at Saint Laurent within the Kering group, where other major luxury houses have had to renew their artistic direction. This longevity sums it all up. His departure would mark the end of an era at Saint Laurent.

article_title: Former Abercrombie & Fitch CMO Carey Collins Krug moves to Vuori
sub_title: Carey Collins Krug, former Abercrombie & Fitch CMO, has been appointed Chief Marketing Officer at activewear brand Vuori, effective October 5, 2026.
article_content: American activewear brand Vuori has appointed retail industry executive Carey Collins Krug as its new chief marketing officer, effective October 5, 2026. In her new role, Krug will lead the company’s global marketing organisation. Her responsibilities include overseeing brand, creative, consumer engagement, digital, retail, wholesale and integrated marketing strategies. She will focus on advancing the global marketing strategy of the business while strengthening connection across sales channels. “Carey brings the kind of brand-building, consumer engagement and cross-functional marketing leadership that will be instrumental as Vuori enters its next chapter of growth,” said Vuori founder and chief executive officer Joe Kudla. “Her experience helping global lifestyle brands sharpen their storytelling and build deeper connections with consumers aligns closely with where we’re headed as we continue to scale.” Krug joins the Encinitas-based business from apparel retailer Abercrombie & Fitch, where she served as chief marketing officer. During her tenure, she played a role in repositioning the brand, driving digital transformation and engaging a new generation of consumers. Earlier in her career, Krug held senior marketing roles at jewelry brand David Yurman, Ralph Lauren and Donna Karan International. "Vuori has a rare combination of brand clarity, product strength and deep consumer connection," said Krug. "The foundation is already there - a powerful brand and an engaged community. I am thrilled to build upon this momentum and scale globally with intentionality and consistency.” Founded in 2015, Vuori creates performance apparel and activewear styles. The company currently operates in close to 30 countries worldwide through its own store network, e-commerce platform and wholesale retail partners.

article_title: CaaStle founder sentenced to five years for securities fraud
sub_title: CaaStle founder Christine Hunsicker received a five-year prison sentence for securities fraud, defrauding investors of nearly $300 million.
article_content: Christine Hunsicker, founder and former CEO of fashion-tech company CaaStle, has been sentenced to five years in prison for securities fraud after admitting to a scheme that defrauded hundreds of investors of nearly 300 million dollars. Hunsicker pleaded guilty earlier this year to one count of securities fraud. According to the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, she falsely presented CaaStle as a rapidly growing business valued at more than 1.4 billion dollars, despite knowing the company was facing financial difficulties. Alongside the five-year prison sentence, Hunsicker has been ordered to serve three years of supervised release and pay 283.3 million dollars in both forfeiture and restitution. Between 2019 and 2025, Hunsicker provided investors with falsified financial statements, fake audits, fabricated bank records and other documents that overstated CaaStle’s revenue, profits and available cash. She also misrepresented how some investment funds would be used, claiming they would purchase shares from existing shareholders when the shareholders themselves had been fabricated. US attorney Jamie McDonald described the case as a “large-scale fraud” and said Hunsicker had promoted the company as a “billion-dollar success”. Hunsicker continued attempting to raise capital even after being removed as CaaStle chair in December 2024. CaaStle, which had previously worked with fashion brands like LK Bennett and Derek Lam to provide rental services, ultimately filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2025.

article_title: Lululemon updates regional leadership structure in Asia
sub_title: Lululemon announces leadership changes in Asia, promoting San Yan Ng to regional president of China and APAC and hiring Jeffrey Hang as SVP and GM of APAC.
article_content: Canadian athletic apparel brand Lululemon has announced two leadership updates to support its continued expansion across China and Asia Pacific (APAC). After eight years serving as general manager of Lululemon's China business, San Yan Ng has been promoted to regional president of China and APAC. Her responsibilities now span both regions. In addition, Jeffrey Hang has joined the company as senior vice president and general manager of APAC. Hang brings extensive experience leading consumer and retail businesses in the region. "China and APAC are home to some of the world's most dynamic consumer markets and are important regions for Lululemon," said André Maestrini, interim co-chief executive officer, president, and chief commercial officer at Lululemon. "As we continue to strategically increase our presence in these markets, we are pleased to promote San Yan to an expanded role and welcome Jeffrey to Lululemon. Together, their strong leadership and track records of success will help us to strengthen our local relevance in the region and grow our community of guests around the world.” Bringing China and APAC under a shared leadership structure will enable Lululemon to better leverage market insights, scale capabilities, and continue delivering experiences that resonate with guests across diverse cultures and communities. As regional president of China and APAC, San Yan Ng leads and drives Lululemon's strategy across both regions. Her new role strengthens alignment between the company's China and APAC businesses, while ensuring the organisation remains closely connected to the unique needs of each market. "I am honored to take on this expanded role and continue working alongside our talented teams in China and APAC," said San Yan Ng. "Both regions present tremendous opportunities, shaped by distinct guest needs, cultures, and market dynamics. By drawing on the strengths of our teams and staying focused on what matters most to our guests, we can continue to create meaningful impact across the business." San Yan Ng joined Lululemon in January 2018 and played a pivotal role in building its business in China, helping to grow it into one of the company's key international markets. Combined with her previous leadership experience across China and the broader Asia Pacific region, she brings a unique perspective and strong understanding of the consumers, markets, and trends shaping the future of the region. Hang joins Lululemon after more than two decades leading premium brands in Asia Pacific and China. Most recently, he served as managing director for Italian luxury brand Bulgari across Southeast Asia, India, Australia, and New Zealand. Prior to that, he was senior vice president and chief executive officer of French luxury label Louis Vuitton China. Having lived and worked in China Mainland, Hong Kong SAR, Macau SAR, Singapore, and Japan, Hang brings broad regional expertise and insight into the diverse markets Lululemon serves in APAC. As senior vice president and general manager of APAC, Hang leads Lululemon's teams in the region with a focus on accelerating growth, strengthening the brand's presence, and supporting long-term ambitions. He reports to Ng. "I am delighted to join Lululemon at a key moment in the company's growth journey," said Hang. "Lululemon has built a strong foundation in Asia Pacific through innovative products, a purpose-led culture, and deep connections with its guests and communities. I look forward to learning from our incredible teams in the region and helping shape the next chapter of success together."

sub_title: Abercrombie & Fitch announces Mary Fox's election to its board of directors, effective August 18, 2026.
article_content: US specialty retailer Abercrombie & Fitch has announced the election of Mary Fox to its board of directors, effective August 18, 2026. sub_title: Erin Magee is leaving Supreme after 22 years, most recently as chief creative officer. She also founded the label MadeMe.
article_content: Automated translation Erin Magee appears to be leaving Supreme after 22 years. Emory stepped down in August 2023, making allegations of structural racism in his resignation letter, which the company denied. The position has not been publicly filled since. Since October 2024, Supreme has been owned by the French-Italian eyewear group EssilorLuxottica, which acquired the brand from VF Corporation (VF Corp) for 1.5 billion dollars. article_title: Farfetch appoints Manny Suero as VP of private client, Americas
sub_title: Farfetch appoints Manny Suero as VP of private client, Americas, to strengthen relations with high-value customers in the region.
article_content: Luxury e-tailer Farfetch has appointed Manny Suero as its new vice president of private client, Americas, as part of efforts to strengthen relations with high-value customers across the region. Suero, who will oversee the expansion of Farfetch’s private client community across the US, Mexico, Brazil and Canada, brings more than 15 years of experience in luxury e-commerce and client relations to the role, most recently serving as director of personal shopping and client relations at Mytheresa. His previous roles also include director of client experience at Olivela, US sales manager at Moda Operandi and head of personal shopping at Yoox Net-A-Porter Group, where he began his career in personal shopping, moving through several roles before moving into senior leadership positions. The US, meanwhile, remains Farfetch’s largest market by active users. Suero’s appointment contributes to Farfetch’s wider turnaround under owner Coupang, which acquired the platform in 2023 and has since sought to refocus the business on its central marketplace model and personalised customer experience.

sub_title: Mathilde Favier, Dior's international PR director, died at 57 in a car accident. Her partner also died. Dior released a statement.

Dior announced the death in a statement describing Favier as "an exceptional woman whose communicative joy, talent and loyalty were exemplary." “Mathilde loved life with a passion. With the passing of Mathilde, Dior is losing an incredible professional, and I have lost a loyal friend. Her optimism and courage commanded admiration. We will sorely miss her smile and her talent. I feel deeply saddened today; my thoughts are very much with her children, her mother, her sisters, her family, her many friends and her team she loved so much," Delphine Arnault, chairman and chief executive officer of Christian Dior Couture, said in the statement. Jonathan Anderson, creative director of Dior, said he is "heartbroken" by Favier's passing. " “We all owe so much to her work and dedication. She brought such warmth, energy and was the most positive and uplifting person I have ever met. Mathilde was the very embodiment of elegance and in many ways, the spirit of Couture itself," he said in a statement. Bernard Arnault, CEO of LVMH, said he was “deeply saddened to learn of the tragic and sudden passing of Mathilde Favier, who devoted so many years to putting her passion, energy and talent at the service of the House of Dior." article_title: CaaStle founder sentenced to five years for securities fraud
sub_title: CaaStle founder Christine Hunsicker received a five-year prison sentence for securities fraud, defrauding investors of nearly $300 million.
article_content: Christine Hunsicker, founder and former CEO of fashion-tech company CaaStle, has been sentenced to five years in prison for securities fraud after admitting to a scheme that defrauded hundreds of investors of nearly 300 million dollars. Hunsicker pleaded guilty earlier this year to one count of securities fraud. According to the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, she falsely presented CaaStle as a rapidly growing business valued at more than 1.4 billion dollars, despite knowing the company was facing financial difficulties. Alongside the five-year prison sentence, Hunsicker has been ordered to serve three years of supervised release and pay 283.3 million dollars in both forfeiture and restitution. Between 2019 and 2025, Hunsicker provided investors with falsified financial statements, fake audits, fabricated bank records and other documents that overstated CaaStle’s revenue, profits and available cash. She also misrepresented how some investment funds would be used, claiming they would purchase shares from existing shareholders when the shareholders themselves had been fabricated. US attorney Jamie McDonald described the case as a “large-scale fraud” and said Hunsicker had promoted the company as a “billion-dollar success”. Hunsicker continued attempting to raise capital even after being removed as CaaStle chair in December 2024. CaaStle, which had previously worked with fashion brands like LK Bennett and Derek Lam to provide rental services, ultimately filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2025.

article_title: Lululemon updates regional leadership structure in Asia

article_title: Erin Magee seemingly steps down as chief creative officer of Supreme
sub_title: Erin Magee is leaving Supreme after 22 years, most recently as chief creative officer. She also founded the label MadeMe.
article_content: Automated translation Erin Magee appears to be leaving Supreme after 22 years. article_title: Kickz: new general manager comes from Zalando

article_title: PrettyLittleThing founder Umar Kamani to launch new fashion and wellness brand
sub_title: Umar Kamani, PrettyLittleThing founder, is launching a new fashion and wellness brand, currently assembling a team in Dubai for international expansion.
article_content:
Umar Kamani, founder of fast fashion e-tailer PrettyLittleThing, is preparing to launch a new consumer brand sitting at the intersection of fashion and wellness, yet little is currently known about the business. article_title: Mathilde Favier, Dior's PR director, dies at 57
sub_title: Mathilde Favier, Dior's international PR director, died at 57 in a car accident. Her partner also died. Dior released a statement.
article_content: Mathilde Favier, director of public relations at Christian Dior Couture , died on Monday, in a car accident in western France. She was 57. Favier's partner, film producer Nicolas Altmayer, 61, also died in the crash. The accident happened around 4 p.m. on the D938 road in Airvault, in the Deux-Sèvres department, when their car collided head-on with a heavy goods vehicle while overtaking another vehicle, according to Nicolas Leclainche, deputy prosecutor at the Niort prosecutor's office, as reported by French regional broadcaster ICI. The prosecutor's office has opened an investigation for involuntary manslaughter by a driver to establish the exact circumstances. Dior announced the death in a statement describing Favier as "an exceptional woman whose communicative joy, talent and loyalty were exemplary." “Mathilde loved life with a passion. With the passing of Mathilde, Dior is losing an incredible professional, and I have lost a loyal friend. Her optimism and courage commanded admiration. We will sorely miss her smile and her talent. I feel deeply saddened today; my thoughts are very much with her children, her mother, her sisters, her family, her many friends and her team she loved so much," Delphine Arnault, chairman and chief executive officer of Christian Dior Couture, said in the statement. Jonathan Anderson, creative director of Dior, said he is "heartbroken" by Favier's passing. " “We all owe so much to her work and dedication. She brought such warmth, energy and was the most positive and uplifting person I have ever met. Mathilde was the very embodiment of elegance and in many ways, the spirit of Couture itself," he said in a statement. Bernard Arnault, CEO of LVMH, said he was “deeply saddened to learn of the tragic and sudden passing of Mathilde Favier, who devoted so many years to putting her passion, energy and talent at the service of the House of Dior." "My heartfelt condolences go to her family and loved ones," Arnault said. Favier had overseen celebrity relations at Christian Dior Couture for 13 years, joining after roles at Glamour magazine and at Italian fashion house Prada. She is the half-sister of Victoire de Castellane, Dior's creative director of fine jewelry; the two got their start in fashion together at French house Chanel through their uncle, Gilles Dufour, who worked alongside designer Karl Lagerfeld. Beyond her Dior role, Favier published two books, "Mathilde à Paris" and "Living Beautifully in Paris." Altmayer, her partner, was a prominent figure in French cinema in his own right. He produced the "OSS 117" and "Brice de Nice" comedies with actor Jean Dujardin, and co-led production company Mandarin & Compagnie with his brother, Éric.

article_title: Anthony Vaccarello's decade at Saint Laurent: A retrospective
sub_title: As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 1...
article_content: Automated translation As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 10-year career with the Kering group as artistic director for the house of Saint Laurent. It was a high-risk succession. Slimane had been untouchable since the Dior Hommes miracle. He transformed Saint Laurent by removing the first name Yves, giving the brand his own rock aesthetic and crowning his approach with economic success. Turnover almost tripled under the Slimane era, rising from 353.7 million euros in 2011, the year before his arrival, to 974 million euros in 2015, according to the annual reports of PPR/Kering. At the time, Vaccarello was 34 years old and closed his own house to devote himself to Saint Laurent. His time at Versus Versace was his most visible experience at a major house. His first spring/summer 2017 show was therefore highly anticipated and scrutinised by a fashion world always eager for commentary. He followed in the footsteps of his predecessor – with black, leather and transparency – and those of the original couturier, Yves Saint Laurent – the tuxedo, 80s shoulders, leopard print, gold lamé and the YSL/Cassandre monogram. For the spring/summer 2018 collection show, Anthony Vaccarello set up at the Trocadéro, with the illuminated Eiffel Tower as a backdrop. This first visual signature orchestrated the brand's international influence: Saint Laurent is Paris, Paris is Saint Laurent. It was not until the young artistic director met Yves Saint Laurent's muse and best friend, Betty Catroux, that the artistic spark was truly ignited. Anthony Vaccarello met her at the inauguration of the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Marrakech. “She is Saint Laurent as she breathes. Her allure, her mystery, her scandalous side, an elusive and desirable danger, all contribute to the aura of this house. You understand the scale of it when you meet Betty,” explained Vaccarello in the context of an exhibition dedicated to this muse in 2020, at the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Paris. Just as the Saint Laurent/Bergé duo embodied the Parisian Rive Gauche, Vaccarello has made the Rive Droite his own. At the end of his career, Yves Saint Laurent said: “I am just a name. A perfume, a lipstick, a pair of tights”. At the beginning of his, Vaccarello expanded the Saint Laurent universe to include lifestyle and developed a brand image that includes art, photography, music, design and various collaborations. Like a conductor, he put his name to the architectural design of Saint Laurent Rive Droite. On the eve of the Covid-19 crisis, Vaccarello presented a show dominated by red, a premonitory colour that would be found in social news. For autumn/winter 2020/2021, the red is as ardent as the bourgeois woman who cheats the monotony of her days with torrid nights. Vaccarello presents this stage as “a defining moment in the definition of his Saint Laurent woman” (W Magazine, 2025). Classic jackets, pussy-bow blouses, lace, vinyl, latex: Vaccarello explores the inherent sensuality of the Saint Laurent woman. Between glamour and provocation, this power of seduction was then imposed in all his campaigns. From spring/summer 2023, the artistic director evolved the Saint Laurent man. To design his wardrobe, he once again drew on the heritage of Betty Catroux and her masculine-feminine style. Pussy-bow blouses, jackets worn next to the skin, leopard prints, soft fabrics, drapes, asymmetries, transparent shirts and fluid trousers are all distinctive signs of a deconstructed man. Six years after Anthony Vaccarello's arrival as artistic director, Saint Laurent crossed the three billion euro turnover threshold for the first time. Sales reached 3.3 billion euros in 2022, compared to 1.22 billion in 2016. At the same time, recurring operating income exceeded one billion euros, for a margin of 30.9 percent. Source: Kering annual results. The first couture house to venture into film financing, Saint Laurent under the Vaccarello era began with a first short film, “Strange Way of Life”, by Madrid-based director Pedro Almodóvar. The masterstroke came at the 2023 Cannes Film Festival, with three films in competition, including “Emilia Pérez” by Jacques Audiard, which won numerous awards, including the Jury Prize and the collective Best Actress award at Cannes. Some say that the branded costumes (the famous Rive Gauche T-shirt worn by Selena Gomez in Emilia Pérez) and the polished aesthetic blur the line between the director's artistic choices and the brand's expression. The tone has been set: Vaccarello has invented a way of investing in cinema other than product placement. Vaccarello celebrates 10 years at Saint Laurent within the Kering group, where other major luxury houses have had to renew their artistic direction. This longevity sums it all up. His departure would mark the end of an era at Saint Laurent.

article_title: Ecco promotes Americas CEO and appoints new product chief
sub_title: Ecco promotes Americas CEO Neal Taylor to the global management team and appoints Adam Meek, formerly of Dr. Martens, as the new product chief.
article_content: Automated translation Ecco has promoted its CEO of the Americas, Neal Taylor, appointing him to the global management team. Taylor has served as executive vice president and chief commercial officer at Ecco Global since August, as he announced on LinkedIn on Tuesday. He works on a hybrid basis from Salem, New Hampshire, from where he has led the Americas region as CEO since March of last year. Before joining Ecco, Taylor worked at the US textile group Hanesbrands Inc., which was acquired by the Canadian apparel group Gildan Activewear Inc. about a year ago. There, he served as senior vice president of global commercial. He also held various management positions at the US sports brand Reebok from 2007 to 2022. Adam Meek has also joined the management team as of August, alongside Taylor. The team includes chief financial officer Marco Bossen and CEO Thomas Gøgsig. article_title: PrettyLittleThing founder Umar Kamani to launch new fashion and wellness brand
sub_title: Umar Kamani, PrettyLittleThing founder, is launching a new fashion and wellness brand, currently assembling a team in Dubai for international expansion.
article_content:
Umar Kamani, founder of fast fashion e-tailer PrettyLittleThing, is preparing to launch a new consumer brand sitting at the intersection of fashion and wellness, yet little is currently known about the business. Kamani revealed the plans on LinkedIn, saying he is “building my next consumer brand” and is currently assembling a creative team in Dubai, with ambitions to expand internationally.
He has not yet revealed the new brand’s name, launch date, product range or business model. “Nothing beats the feeling of building and the excitement of what’s to come,” he said, adding that he is looking for “team players” who “demand the best of themselves” to help develop the business. A separate recruitment post shared by Kamani on Instagram provided further details, with the founding team being built from the ground up in Dubai. Roles currently being recruited for include fashion designers and buyers, digital and social, creative, third-party logistics and distribution, finance and other founding positions. Kamani co-founded PrettyLittleThing alongside his brother Adam Kamani in 2012 at the age of 24. Debenhams Group - formerly Boohoo Group - acquired a 66 percent stake in the business in 2017 before buying the remaining 34 percent in 2020 in a deal worth up to 323.8 million pounds. In 2023, Kamani stepped down as PLT chief executive before announcing his return to the business in 2024 under an undisclosed title. More recently, PLT has undergone a significant turnaround under Debenhams Group, returning to profitability in FY26 with adjusted EBITDA of 14 million pounds, compared with a one million pound loss the previous year.

article_title: Farfetch appoints Manny Suero as VP of private client, Americas
sub_title: Farfetch appoints Manny Suero as VP of private client, Americas, to strengthen relations with high-value customers in the region.
article_content: Luxury e-tailer Farfetch has appointed Manny Suero as its new vice president of private client, Americas, as part of efforts to strengthen relations with high-value customers across the region. Suero, who will oversee the expansion of Farfetch’s private client community across the US, Mexico, Brazil and Canada, brings more than 15 years of experience in luxury e-commerce and client relations to the role, most recently serving as director of personal shopping and client relations at Mytheresa. His previous roles also include director of client experience at Olivela, US sales manager at Moda Operandi and head of personal shopping at Yoox Net-A-Porter Group, where he began his career in personal shopping, moving through several roles before moving into senior leadership positions. The appointment comes as Farfetch more directly targets its top-tier customers, known internally as Extremely Important Customers (EICs), who account for a significant share of the platform’s revenue. The US, meanwhile, remains Farfetch’s largest market by active users. Suero’s appointment contributes to Farfetch’s wider turnaround under owner Coupang, which acquired the platform in 2023 and has since sought to refocus the business on its central marketplace model and personalised customer experience.

article_title: Mathilde Favier, Dior's PR director, dies at 57
sub_title: Mathilde Favier, Dior's international PR director, died at 57 in a car accident. Her partner also died. Dior released a statement.
article_content: Mathilde Favier, director of public relations at Christian Dior Couture , died on Monday, in a car accident in western France. She was 57. Favier's partner, film producer Nicolas Altmayer, 61, also died in the crash. The accident happened around 4 p.m. on the D938 road in Airvault, in the Deux-Sèvres department, when their car collided head-on with a heavy goods vehicle while overtaking another vehicle, according to Nicolas Leclainche, deputy prosecutor at the Niort prosecutor's office, as reported by French regional broadcaster ICI. The prosecutor's office has opened an investigation for involuntary manslaughter by a driver to establish the exact circumstances. Dior announced the death in a statement describing Favier as "an exceptional woman whose communicative joy, talent and loyalty were exemplary." “Mathilde loved life with a passion. With the passing of Mathilde, Dior is losing an incredible professional, and I have lost a loyal friend. Her optimism and courage commanded admiration. We will sorely miss her smile and her talent. I feel deeply saddened today; my thoughts are very much with her children, her mother, her sisters, her family, her many friends and her team she loved so much," Delphine Arnault, chairman and chief executive officer of Christian Dior Couture, said in the statement. Jonathan Anderson, creative director of Dior, said he is "heartbroken" by Favier's passing. " “We all owe so much to her work and dedication. She brought such warmth, energy and was the most positive and uplifting person I have ever met. Mathilde was the very embodiment of elegance and in many ways, the spirit of Couture itself," he said in a statement. Bernard Arnault, CEO of LVMH, said he was “deeply saddened to learn of the tragic and sudden passing of Mathilde Favier, who devoted so many years to putting her passion, energy and talent at the service of the House of Dior." "My heartfelt condolences go to her family and loved ones," Arnault said. Favier had overseen celebrity relations at Christian Dior Couture for 13 years, joining after roles at Glamour magazine and at Italian fashion house Prada. She is the half-sister of Victoire de Castellane, Dior's creative director of fine jewelry; the two got their start in fashion together at French house Chanel through their uncle, Gilles Dufour, who worked alongside designer Karl Lagerfeld. Beyond her Dior role, Favier published two books, "Mathilde à Paris" and "Living Beautifully in Paris." Altmayer, her partner, was a prominent figure in French cinema in his own right. He produced the "OSS 117" and "Brice de Nice" comedies with actor Jean Dujardin, and co-led production company Mandarin & Compagnie with his brother, Éric.

article_title: Anthony Vaccarello's decade at Saint Laurent: A retrospective
sub_title: As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 1...
article_content: Automated translation As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 10-year career with the Kering group as artistic director for the house of Saint Laurent. It was a high-risk succession. Slimane had been untouchable since the Dior Hommes miracle. He transformed Saint Laurent by removing the first name Yves, giving the brand his own rock aesthetic and crowning his approach with economic success. Turnover almost tripled under the Slimane era, rising from 353.7 million euros in 2011, the year before his arrival, to 974 million euros in 2015, according to the annual reports of PPR/Kering. At the time, Vaccarello was 34 years old and closed his own house to devote himself to Saint Laurent. His time at Versus Versace was his most visible experience at a major house. His first spring/summer 2017 show was therefore highly anticipated and scrutinised by a fashion world always eager for commentary. He followed in the footsteps of his predecessor – with black, leather and transparency – and those of the original couturier, Yves Saint Laurent – the tuxedo, 80s shoulders, leopard print, gold lamé and the YSL/Cassandre monogram. For the spring/summer 2018 collection show, Anthony Vaccarello set up at the Trocadéro, with the illuminated Eiffel Tower as a backdrop. This first visual signature orchestrated the brand's international influence: Saint Laurent is Paris, Paris is Saint Laurent. It was not until the young artistic director met Yves Saint Laurent's muse and best friend, Betty Catroux, that the artistic spark was truly ignited. Anthony Vaccarello met her at the inauguration of the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Marrakech. “She is Saint Laurent as she breathes. Her allure, her mystery, her scandalous side, an elusive and desirable danger, all contribute to the aura of this house. You understand the scale of it when you meet Betty,” explained Vaccarello in the context of an exhibition dedicated to this muse in 2020, at the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Paris. Just as the Saint Laurent/Bergé duo embodied the Parisian Rive Gauche, Vaccarello has made the Rive Droite his own. At the end of his career, Yves Saint Laurent said: “I am just a name. A perfume, a lipstick, a pair of tights”. At the beginning of his, Vaccarello expanded the Saint Laurent universe to include lifestyle and developed a brand image that includes art, photography, music, design and various collaborations. Like a conductor, he put his name to the architectural design of Saint Laurent Rive Droite. On the eve of the Covid-19 crisis, Vaccarello presented a show dominated by red, a premonitory colour that would be found in social news. For autumn/winter 2020/2021, the red is as ardent as the bourgeois woman who cheats the monotony of her days with torrid nights. Vaccarello presents this stage as “a defining moment in the definition of his Saint Laurent woman” (W Magazine, 2025). Classic jackets, pussy-bow blouses, lace, vinyl, latex: Vaccarello explores the inherent sensuality of the Saint Laurent woman. Between glamour and provocation, this power of seduction was then imposed in all his campaigns. From spring/summer 2023, the artistic director evolved the Saint Laurent man. To design his wardrobe, he once again drew on the heritage of Betty Catroux and her masculine-feminine style. Pussy-bow blouses, jackets worn next to the skin, leopard prints, soft fabrics, drapes, asymmetries, transparent shirts and fluid trousers are all distinctive signs of a deconstructed man. Six years after Anthony Vaccarello's arrival as artistic director, Saint Laurent crossed the three billion euro turnover threshold for the first time. Sales reached 3.3 billion euros in 2022, compared to 1.22 billion in 2016. At the same time, recurring operating income exceeded one billion euros, for a margin of 30.9 percent. Source: Kering annual results. The first couture house to venture into film financing, Saint Laurent under the Vaccarello era began with a first short film, “Strange Way of Life”, by Madrid-based director Pedro Almodóvar. The masterstroke came at the 2023 Cannes Film Festival, with three films in competition, including “Emilia Pérez” by Jacques Audiard, which won numerous awards, including the Jury Prize and the collective Best Actress award at Cannes. Some say that the branded costumes (the famous Rive Gauche T-shirt worn by Selena Gomez in Emilia Pérez) and the polished aesthetic blur the line between the director's artistic choices and the brand's expression. The tone has been set: Vaccarello has invented a way of investing in cinema other than product placement. Vaccarello celebrates 10 years at Saint Laurent within the Kering group, where other major luxury houses have had to renew their artistic direction. This longevity sums it all up. His departure would mark the end of an era at Saint Laurent.

article_title: Former Abercrombie & Fitch CMO Carey Collins Krug moves to Vuori
sub_title: Carey Collins Krug, former Abercrombie & Fitch CMO, has been appointed Chief Marketing Officer at activewear brand Vuori, effective October 5, 2026.
article_content: American activewear brand Vuori has appointed retail industry executive Carey Collins Krug as its new chief marketing officer, effective October 5, 2026. In her new role, Krug will lead the company’s global marketing organisation. Her responsibilities include overseeing brand, creative, consumer engagement, digital, retail, wholesale and integrated marketing strategies. She will focus on advancing the global marketing strategy of the business while strengthening connection across sales channels. “Carey brings the kind of brand-building, consumer engagement and cross-functional marketing leadership that will be instrumental as Vuori enters its next chapter of growth,” said Vuori founder and chief executive officer Joe Kudla. “Her experience helping global lifestyle brands sharpen their storytelling and build deeper connections with consumers aligns closely with where we’re headed as we continue to scale.” Krug joins the Encinitas-based business from apparel retailer Abercrombie & Fitch, where she served as chief marketing officer. During her tenure, she played a role in repositioning the brand, driving digital transformation and engaging a new generation of consumers. Earlier in her career, Krug held senior marketing roles at jewelry brand David Yurman, Ralph Lauren and Donna Karan International. "Vuori has a rare combination of brand clarity, product strength and deep consumer connection," said Krug. "The foundation is already there - a powerful brand and an engaged community. I am thrilled to build upon this momentum and scale globally with intentionality and consistency.” Founded in 2015, Vuori creates performance apparel and activewear styles. The company currently operates in close to 30 countries worldwide through its own store network, e-commerce platform and wholesale retail partners.

article_title: New board member: Mary Fox joins Abercrombie & Fitch
sub_title: Abercrombie & Fitch announces Mary Fox's election to its board of directors, effective August 18, 2026.
article_content: US specialty retailer Abercrombie & Fitch has announced the election of Mary Fox to its board of directors, effective August 18, 2026. Fox, 54, currently serves as president of home furnishings firm The Lovesac Company, where she oversees operations, marketing, finance, human resources, and overall business performance. “We are excited to welcome Mary to Abercrombie & Fitch Co.’s Board of Directors. She brings an incredibly strong digital commerce and brand-building background that spans a 25-year career in consumer goods. As a current executive, she brings a deep understanding of today’s dynamic consumer environment and how customers are connecting with brands, which will be an invaluable addition to the Board and company,” said Nigel Travis, chairperson of the board. Prior to joining Lovesac, she served as general manager for North American consumer products at BIC and held senior roles at French cosmetics group L’Oréal across e-commerce, business development, and business transformation over six years. She also spent more than a decade at Walmart in expanding roles across private label apparel, merchandising, brand management, strategy, mergers and acquisitions, and global sourcing. Fox commented: “I’m thrilled to join Abercrombie & Fitch Co.’s Board of Directors. Having long admired the company’s performance and reputation as leaders in the apparel and retail industries, I look forward to partnering with CEO Fran Horowitz and her management team, as well as Nigel and the Board as the company continues its work to achieve its long-term ambitions to continue delivering diversified, global growth.”

article_title: CaaStle founder sentenced to five years for securities fraud
sub_title: CaaStle founder Christine Hunsicker received a five-year prison sentence for securities fraud, defrauding investors of nearly $300 million.
article_content: Christine Hunsicker, founder and former CEO of fashion-tech company CaaStle, has been sentenced to five years in prison for securities fraud after admitting to a scheme that defrauded hundreds of investors of nearly 300 million dollars. Hunsicker pleaded guilty earlier this year to one count of securities fraud. According to the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, she falsely presented CaaStle as a rapidly growing business valued at more than 1.4 billion dollars, despite knowing the company was facing financial difficulties. Alongside the five-year prison sentence, Hunsicker has been ordered to serve three years of supervised release and pay 283.3 million dollars in both forfeiture and restitution. Between 2019 and 2025, Hunsicker provided investors with falsified financial statements, fake audits, fabricated bank records and other documents that overstated CaaStle’s revenue, profits and available cash. She also misrepresented how some investment funds would be used, claiming they would purchase shares from existing shareholders when the shareholders themselves had been fabricated. US attorney Jamie McDonald described the case as a “large-scale fraud” and said Hunsicker had promoted the company as a “billion-dollar success”. Hunsicker continued attempting to raise capital even after being removed as CaaStle chair in December 2024. CaaStle, which had previously worked with fashion brands like LK Bennett and Derek Lam to provide rental services, ultimately filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2025.

article_title: Lululemon updates regional leadership structure in Asia
sub_title: Lululemon announces leadership changes in Asia, promoting San Yan Ng to regional president of China and APAC and hiring Jeffrey Hang as SVP and GM of APAC.
article_content: Canadian athletic apparel brand Lululemon has announced two leadership updates to support its continued expansion across China and Asia Pacific (APAC). After eight years serving as general manager of Lululemon's China business, San Yan Ng has been promoted to regional president of China and APAC. Her responsibilities now span both regions. In addition, Jeffrey Hang has joined the company as senior vice president and general manager of APAC. Hang brings extensive experience leading consumer and retail businesses in the region. "China and APAC are home to some of the world's most dynamic consumer markets and are important regions for Lululemon," said André Maestrini, interim co-chief executive officer, president, and chief commercial officer at Lululemon. "As we continue to strategically increase our presence in these markets, we are pleased to promote San Yan to an expanded role and welcome Jeffrey to Lululemon. Together, their strong leadership and track records of success will help us to strengthen our local relevance in the region and grow our community of guests around the world.” Bringing China and APAC under a shared leadership structure will enable Lululemon to better leverage market insights, scale capabilities, and continue delivering experiences that resonate with guests across diverse cultures and communities. As regional president of China and APAC, San Yan Ng leads and drives Lululemon's strategy across both regions. Her new role strengthens alignment between the company's China and APAC businesses, while ensuring the organisation remains closely connected to the unique needs of each market. "I am honored to take on this expanded role and continue working alongside our talented teams in China and APAC," said San Yan Ng. "Both regions present tremendous opportunities, shaped by distinct guest needs, cultures, and market dynamics. By drawing on the strengths of our teams and staying focused on what matters most to our guests, we can continue to create meaningful impact across the business." San Yan Ng joined Lululemon in January 2018 and played a pivotal role in building its business in China, helping to grow it into one of the company's key international markets. Combined with her previous leadership experience across China and the broader Asia Pacific region, she brings a unique perspective and strong understanding of the consumers, markets, and trends shaping the future of the region. Hang joins Lululemon after more than two decades leading premium brands in Asia Pacific and China. Most recently, he served as managing director for Italian luxury brand Bulgari across Southeast Asia, India, Australia, and New Zealand. Prior to that, he was senior vice president and chief executive officer of French luxury label Louis Vuitton China. Having lived and worked in China Mainland, Hong Kong SAR, Macau SAR, Singapore, and Japan, Hang brings broad regional expertise and insight into the diverse markets Lululemon serves in APAC. As senior vice president and general manager of APAC, Hang leads Lululemon's teams in the region with a focus on accelerating growth, strengthening the brand's presence, and supporting long-term ambitions. He reports to Ng. "I am delighted to join Lululemon at a key moment in the company's growth journey," said Hang. "Lululemon has built a strong foundation in Asia Pacific through innovative products, a purpose-led culture, and deep connections with its guests and communities. I look forward to learning from our incredible teams in the region and helping shape the next chapter of success together."

article_title: Anthony Vaccarello's decade at Saint Laurent: A retrospective
sub_title: As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 1...
article_content: Automated translation As a rumour circulates on social media that Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent, FashionUnited looks back at the key moments that have marked his 10-year career with the Kering group as artistic director for the house of Saint Laurent. It was a high-risk succession. Slimane had been untouchable since the Dior Hommes miracle. He transformed Saint Laurent by removing the first name Yves, giving the brand his own rock aesthetic and crowning his approach with economic success. Turnover almost tripled under the Slimane era, rising from 353.7 million euros in 2011, the year before his arrival, to 974 million euros in 2015, according to the annual reports of PPR/Kering. At the time, Vaccarello was 34 years old and closed his own house to devote himself to Saint Laurent. His time at Versus Versace was his most visible experience at a major house. His first spring/summer 2017 show was therefore highly anticipated and scrutinised by a fashion world always eager for commentary. He followed in the footsteps of his predecessor – with black, leather and transparency – and those of the original couturier, Yves Saint Laurent – the tuxedo, 80s shoulders, leopard print, gold lamé and the YSL/Cassandre monogram. For the spring/summer 2018 collection show, Anthony Vaccarello set up at the Trocadéro, with the illuminated Eiffel Tower as a backdrop. This first visual signature orchestrated the brand's international influence: Saint Laurent is Paris, Paris is Saint Laurent. It was not until the young artistic director met Yves Saint Laurent's muse and best friend, Betty Catroux, that the artistic spark was truly ignited. Anthony Vaccarello met her at the inauguration of the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Marrakech. “She is Saint Laurent as she breathes. Her allure, her mystery, her scandalous side, an elusive and desirable danger, all contribute to the aura of this house. You understand the scale of it when you meet Betty,” explained Vaccarello in the context of an exhibition dedicated to this muse in 2020, at the Yves Saint Laurent museum in Paris. Just as the Saint Laurent/Bergé duo embodied the Parisian Rive Gauche, Vaccarello has made the Rive Droite his own. At the end of his career, Yves Saint Laurent said: “I am just a name. A perfume, a lipstick, a pair of tights”. At the beginning of his, Vaccarello expanded the Saint Laurent universe to include lifestyle and developed a brand image that includes art, photography, music, design and various collaborations. Like a conductor, he put his name to the architectural design of Saint Laurent Rive Droite. On the eve of the Covid-19 crisis, Vaccarello presented a show dominated by red, a premonitory colour that would be found in social news. For autumn/winter 2020/2021, the red is as ardent as the bourgeois woman who cheats the monotony of her days with torrid nights. Vaccarello presents this stage as “a defining moment in the definition of his Saint Laurent woman” (W Magazine, 2025). Classic jackets, pussy-bow blouses, lace, vinyl, latex: Vaccarello explores the inherent sensuality of the Saint Laurent woman. Between glamour and provocation, this power of seduction was then imposed in all his campaigns. From spring/summer 2023, the artistic director evolved the Saint Laurent man. To design his wardrobe, he once again drew on the heritage of Betty Catroux and her masculine-feminine style. Pussy-bow blouses, jackets worn next to the skin, leopard prints, soft fabrics, drapes, asymmetries, transparent shirts and fluid trousers are all distinctive signs of a deconstructed man. Six years after Anthony Vaccarello's arrival as artistic director, Saint Laurent crossed the three billion euro turnover threshold for the first time. Sales reached 3.3 billion euros in 2022, compared to 1.22 billion in 2016. At the same time, recurring operating income exceeded one billion euros, for a margin of 30.9 percent. Source: Kering annual results. The first couture house to venture into film financing, Saint Laurent under the Vaccarello era began with a first short film, “Strange Way of Life”, by Madrid-based director Pedro Almodóvar. The masterstroke came at the 2023 Cannes Film Festival, with three films in competition, including “Emilia Pérez” by Jacques Audiard, which won numerous awards, including the Jury Prize and the collective Best Actress award at Cannes. Some say that the branded costumes (the famous Rive Gauche T-shirt worn by Selena Gomez in Emilia Pérez) and the polished aesthetic blur the line between the director's artistic choices and the brand's expression. The tone has been set: Vaccarello has invented a way of investing in cinema other than product placement. Vaccarello celebrates 10 years at Saint Laurent within the Kering group, where other major luxury houses have had to renew their artistic direction. This longevity sums it all up. His departure would mark the end of an era at Saint Laurent.

article_title: Mathilde Favier, Dior's PR director, dies at 57
sub_title: Mathilde Favier, Dior's international PR director, died at 57 in a car accident. Her partner also died. Dior released a statement.
article_content: Mathilde Favier, director of public relations at Christian Dior Couture , died on Monday, in a car accident in western France. She was 57. Favier's partner, film producer Nicolas Altmayer, 61, also died in the crash. The accident happened around 4 p.m. on the D938 road in Airvault, in the Deux-Sèvres department, when their car collided head-on with a heavy goods vehicle while overtaking another vehicle, according to Nicolas Leclainche, deputy prosecutor at the Niort prosecutor's office, as reported by French regional broadcaster ICI. The prosecutor's office has opened an investigation for involuntary manslaughter by a driver to establish the exact circumstances. Dior announced the death in a statement describing Favier as "an exceptional woman whose communicative joy, talent and loyalty were exemplary." “Mathilde loved life with a passion. With the passing of Mathilde, Dior is losing an incredible professional, and I have lost a loyal friend. Her optimism and courage commanded admiration. We will sorely miss her smile and her talent. I feel deeply saddened today; my thoughts are very much with her children, her mother, her sisters, her family, her many friends and her team she loved so much," Delphine Arnault, chairman and chief executive officer of Christian Dior Couture, said in the statement. Jonathan Anderson, creative director of Dior, said he is "heartbroken" by Favier's passing. " “We all owe so much to her work and dedication. She brought such warmth, energy and was the most positive and uplifting person I have ever met. Mathilde was the very embodiment of elegance and in many ways, the spirit of Couture itself," he said in a statement. Bernard Arnault, CEO of LVMH, said he was “deeply saddened to learn of the tragic and sudden passing of Mathilde Favier, who devoted so many years to putting her passion, energy and talent at the service of the House of Dior." Favier had overseen celebrity relations at Christian Dior Couture for 13 years, joining after roles at Glamour magazine and at Italian fashion house Prada. article_title: CaaStle founder sentenced to five years for securities fraud
sub_title: CaaStle founder Christine Hunsicker received a five-year prison sentence for securities fraud, defrauding investors of nearly $300 million.
article_content: Christine Hunsicker, founder and former CEO of fashion-tech company CaaStle, has been sentenced to five years in prison for securities fraud after admitting to a scheme that defrauded hundreds of investors of nearly 300 million dollars. Hunsicker pleaded guilty earlier this year to one count of securities fraud. According to the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, she falsely presented CaaStle as a rapidly growing business valued at more than 1.4 billion dollars, despite knowing the company was facing financial difficulties. Alongside the five-year prison sentence, Hunsicker has been ordered to serve three years of supervised release and pay 283.3 million dollars in both forfeiture and restitution. Between 2019 and 2025, Hunsicker provided investors with falsified financial statements, fake audits, fabricated bank records and other documents that overstated CaaStle’s revenue, profits and available cash. She also misrepresented how some investment funds would be used, claiming they would purchase shares from existing shareholders when the shareholders themselves had been fabricated. US attorney Jamie McDonald described the case as a “large-scale fraud” and said Hunsicker had promoted the company as a “billion-dollar success”. Hunsicker continued attempting to raise capital even after being removed as CaaStle chair in December 2024. CaaStle, which had previously worked with fashion brands like LK Bennett and Derek Lam to provide rental services, ultimately filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2025.

article_title: Lululemon updates regional leadership structure in Asia
sub_title: Lululemon announces leadership changes in Asia, promoting San Yan Ng to regional president of China and APAC and hiring Jeffrey Hang as SVP and GM of APAC.
article_content: Canadian athletic apparel brand Lululemon has announced two leadership updates to support its continued expansion across China and Asia Pacific (APAC). Her new role strengthens alignment between the company's China and APAC businesses, while ensuring the organisation remains closely connected to the unique needs of each market. "I am honored to take on this expanded role and continue working alongside our talented teams in China and APAC," said San Yan Ng. "Both regions present tremendous opportunities, shaped by distinct guest needs, cultures, and market dynamics. As senior vice president and general manager of APAC, Hang leads Lululemon's teams in the region with a focus on accelerating growth, strengthening the brand's presence, and supporting long-term ambitions. "Lululemon has built a strong foundation in Asia Pacific through innovative products, a purpose-led culture, and deep connections with its guests and communities. I look forward to learning from our incredible teams in the region and helping shape the next chapter of success together."

It was a high-risk succession. Slimane had been untouchable since the Dior Hommes miracle. He transformed Saint Laurent by removing the first name Yves, giving the brand his own rock aesthetic and crowning his approach with economic success. At the time, Vaccarello was 34 years old and closed his own house to devote himself to Saint Laurent. His time at Versus Versace was his most visible experience at a major house. His first spring/summer 2017 show was therefore highly anticipated and scrutinised by a fashion world always eager for commentary. He followed in the footsteps of his predecessor – with black, leather and transparency – and those of the original couturier, Yves Saint Laurent – the tuxedo, 80s shoulders, leopard print, gold lamé and the YSL/Cassandre monogram. For the spring/summer 2018 collection show, Anthony Vaccarello set up at the Trocadéro, with the illuminated Eiffel Tower as a backdrop. This first visual signature orchestrated the brand's international influence: Saint Laurent is Paris, Paris is Saint Laurent. It was not until the young artistic director met Yves Saint Laurent's muse and best friend, Betty Catroux, that the artistic spark was truly ignited.
